record.paper_title: The Statistical Model of Nuclear Reactions: Open Problems
record.context_brief: Strong low-lying gamma channels and neutron-width PTD
record.original_question: A possible way to reconcile the statistical model with the experimental total gamma decay-width data is that a comparatively small number of gamma transitions to low-lying final states are much more strongly coupled than the rest. Such channels would need to be intense enough to shift the simulated total gamma decay widths toward the experimental values and few enough in number to evade the central-limit-theorem narrowing that normally makes the predicted distribution too narrow. The open question is whether a comparatively small number of such strongly coupled gamma decay channels could also change the Porter-Thomas distribution behavior of the reduced neutron widths.

evidence.quote: Given the experimental results, a small number of strong gamma transitions to low-lying final states might offer a way out of the dilemma [3]. These should have sufficient intensity to shift the simulated distribution of total gamma decay widths towards the experimental values. Their number should be sufficiently small to overcome the limits of the central-limit theorem and to broaden the distribution of total gamma decay widths.
It is an open question whether a comparatively small number of such strongly coupled gamma decay channels could also cause a change of the PTD for the reduced neutron widths.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a compound-nucleus resonance described by a statistical model with the following ingredients:

(i) A set of N reduced partial neutron width amplitudes {γ_n^(i)} (i = 1,…,N) attached to N resonances of fixed spin and parity at excitation energies near the neutron separation threshold. In the standard Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) random-matrix description, these amplitudes are independent zero-mean Gaussian random variables, so that the reduced neutron widths Γ_n^(i) ∝ (γ_n^(i))^2 are distributed according to the Porter–Thomas distribution

   P(x) dx = (1/√(2π x)) exp(−x/2) dx,   x = Γ_n^(i)/⟨Γ_n⟩,

i.e. a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.

(ii) A set of gamma decay channels c = 1,…,M from each resonance to lower-lying final states, with partial gamma widths Γ_{γ,c}^(i) and total gamma width Γ_γ^(i) = Σ_c Γ_{γ,c}^(i). In the standard picture the partial-width amplitudes γ_{γ,c}^(i) are also independent zero-mean Gaussian random variables, so each Γ_{γ,c}^(i) is Porter–Thomas distributed and, by the central limit theorem, the total widths Γ_γ^(i) have a relative variance that scales as 1/M_eff and is therefore strongly peaked about its mean for large effective channel number M_eff.

Hypothesis. Suppose now that a small subset S ⊂ {1,…,M} of gamma decay channels (with |S| ≪ M, e.g. transitions to a few low-lying final states) is anomalously strongly coupled, in the sense that the variances ⟨(γ_{γ,c}^(i))^2⟩ for c ∈ S are much larger than the variances for c ∉ S. Assume |S| is small enough that the central-limit-theorem narrowing of the distribution of Γ_γ^(i) is evaded (so the distribution of total gamma widths is broadened toward experimental values), yet large enough in coupling strength to shift the average Γ_γ^(i) toward the experimentally observed values.

Within a unified random-matrix / shell-model statistical framework where neutron and gamma channels are treated on the same footing (e.g. via a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian H_eff = H_GOE − (i/2) Σ_c V_c V_c^T with channel-coupling vectors V_c), the strong gamma channels in S contribute rank-|S| anti-Hermitian terms that break orthogonal invariance and mix the resonances.

Question. Does the presence of such a small number |S| of strongly coupled gamma decay channels — sufficient to broaden the distribution of total gamma decay widths Γ_γ^(i) and shift its mean toward experiment — necessarily induce a measurable deviation of the distribution of normalized reduced neutron widths Γ_n^(i)/⟨Γ_n⟩ from the Porter–Thomas (chi-squared, one degree of freedom) distribution? Quantify the deviation, for instance by computing the effective number of degrees of freedom ν in a fit to a chi-squared distribution of ν degrees of freedom, as a function of |S| and of the coupling strengths of the strong gamma channels.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work has shown that channel coupling can in principle modify the Porter–Thomas distribution: rank-one and few-channel anti-Hermitian perturbations to a GOE Hamiltonian provably alter the chi-squared(1) law for partial widths, and realistic estimates of nonstatistical gamma decay yield significant modifications of the PTD for neutron widths. Experimental evidence in 150Nd indicates branching-ratio statistics inconsistent with ν=1, supporting deviations. However, a definitive quantitative answer linking a small set of strong low-lying gamma transitions to a specific, observed change in the neutron-width PTD across nuclei has not been established, so the question is best regarded as partially addressed but not fully resolved.

status_evidence.title: Neutron Resonance Widths and the Porter-Thomas Distribution
status_evidence.snippet: Two terms in the effective Hamiltonian that violate orthogonal invariance are identified, both due to coupling to decay channels; realistic estimates for coupling to the neutron channel and for non-statistical gamma decays yield significant modifications of the PTD.
status_evidence.claim: Channel coupling, including non-statistical gamma decay, can significantly modify the Porter-Thomas distribution of neutron widths.

status_evidence.title: Deviations from the Porter-Thomas Distribution due to Nonstatistical γ Decay below the 150Nd Neutron Separation Threshold
status_evidence.snippet: Average gamma branching ratio in 150Nd implies an effective chi-squared degree of freedom ν=1.93(12), rejecting the validity of PTD with ν=1.
status_evidence.claim: Experimental data show deviation from PTD attributable to nonstatistical gamma decay.

status_evidence.title: Modification of the Porter-Thomas Distribution by Rank-One Interaction
status_evidence.snippet: Rank-one interaction modifies the Porter-Thomas distribution.
status_evidence.claim: Mathematically, even rank-one channel coupling perturbs the PTD.
